summary.heading: Stage 1: Change is real, and cannot coherently be denied
summary.body:
Feser opens with four everyday changes, one for each kind Aristotelians recognize: coffee cooling (**qualitative**), a leaf falling (**local**, change of place), a puddle growing in the rain (**quantitative**), and a swatted fly dying (**substantial**). The senses show such changes happen. Even if, as in Descartes or *The Matrix*, your whole life were a dream, your **experiences** would still succeed one another — and that is change.

**Parmenides** argued that change is impossible: the coffee’s coldness doesn’t exist while it is hot, so its becoming cold would be something coming from nothing. Feser gives two replies. First, the view is **self-refuting**: reasoning your way to the conclusion that change is unreal means moving from premise to premise — itself a change. Second, Aristotle showed that change does not in fact require something from nothing.

summary.heading: Aristotle’s answer: actuality and potentiality
summary.body: While the coffee is hot, its coldness is not **actual**, but it isn’t nothing either: it is there **potentially**. The coffee can cool, stain the rug, or wake you up; it cannot power an engine, turn into chicken soup, or become a live chicken. That it has some potentials and lacks others shows potentiality is something real and determinate, between full actuality and sheer nothing. So change is **the actualization of a potential** — not something from nothing, because the potential was never nothing.

summary.heading: Change requires a changer: the principle of causality
summary.body: Every change has something that brings it about: the cool air chills the coffee; your wrist drives the swatter. But this isn’t just a generalization from examples; it **follows from what change is**. The coffee’s potential coldness is merely potential, and what is merely potential can’t do anything — only what is actual acts. So a potential can’t actualize itself; something already actual (the cool air, ice cubes) must do it. This is the **principle of causality**: no potential is actualized except by something already actual. Note its scope: it concerns what **goes from potential to actual**, not ‘everything’.

summary.heading: Linear series stretching back in time
summary.body:
Often a changer is itself being changed: the air’s coolness was actualized by the air conditioner; your wrist’s motion by firing neurons. Feser is careful not to claim that every changer must itself be changing — that doesn’t follow and isn’t true. The point is conditional: *if* a cause is changing, its change needs a cause.

So we get series: coffee ← air ← air conditioner ← your pressing the button; fly ← swatter ← wrist ← neurons ← irritation at the buzzing. These run **backward in time**, in a **linear** way. Feser then grants, for argument’s sake, that such a series might be **infinite**, with no first moment — as Aristotle himself believed. Many think the Big Bang disproves that; some physicists speculate about earlier or parallel universes stretching back forever. Feser finds the speculation dubious but says it **doesn’t matter**: the argument works even for a beginningless universe or multiverse.

summary.heading: The hierarchical series: cup, desk, floor, earth
summary.body:
A second kind of series — the **hierarchical** kind — must have a first member. It is easiest to introduce by looking at a single moment (though simultaneity isn’t what defines it). Your cup is three feet up because the desk holds it *now*; the desk is held *now* by the floor, the floor by the foundation, the foundation by the earth. A lamp hangs from a chain, held by a fixture in the ceiling, held by the walls, all at once. Each case involves actualized potentials (the desk actualizes the cup’s potential to be three feet up) without any passage of time.

What makes such a series hierarchical is the **dependence** of later members on earlier ones. The cup can’t stay up on its own; the desk can’t hold it on its own, since it would fall without the floor. In a sense it is the earth doing all the holding, **through intermediaries** that act like **instruments** — as it is the painter, not the brush, who paints. Contrast the linear case: once you switch on the air conditioner, it keeps cooling even if you leave or drop dead. But if the floor collapses, desk and cup fall **at once**.

summary.heading: What ‘first’ means
summary.body:
So a hierarchical series needs a first member, but not ‘first’ in time. Since the intermediaries have no power of their own to hold anything up, the series couldn’t exist unless something could hold them up **without being held up itself**. If they are instruments, something must be using them; if their power is borrowed, something must have it ‘built in’. A first cause here is one whose power is **nonderivative and noninstrumental** — able to actualize without being actualized.

Nor is finitude the point. A paintbrush can’t move itself, and an **infinitely long handle** wouldn’t help; an infinite stack of desks would be as powerless to hold up the cup as one. ‘First’ means **primary** rather than secondary, not ‘the one before the second, third and fourth’. Feser adds that even the earth isn’t truly first in the strict sense — a point that pays off shortly.

summary.heading: Taking stock: the hierarchical series is more fundamental
summary.body: In a linear series each member has its own causal power (the air stays cool and keeps chilling the coffee for a while even after the air conditioner is off). In a hierarchical series, every member but the first has only **derivative** power. The hierarchical kind is harder to grasp at first, because we must abstract the notion of actualizing a potential from everyday change and apply it where time doesn’t matter. But it is **more fundamental**: every linear series presupposes hierarchical ones, which trace to a first cause — indeed a single one. A footnote gives the scholastic labels: linear = ordered **per accidens**; hierarchical = ordered **per se**.

summary.heading: From change to existence: what keeps the coffee in being right now?
summary.body:
The pivotal move: coffee can cool only if it **exists**. What makes it exist — not how it was brewed, but what keeps it existing **here and now**?

Take its water. That matter could exist as separate hydrogen and oxygen, yet right now its potential to be *water* is actualized. Why? A past process that combined the gases explains **how the water got here**; the fact that nothing has split it explains **how it might cease to exist**; neither says what keeps it in existence at this instant. ‘Chemical bonding’ just restates the question (the atoms could be bonded otherwise); atomic structure pushes it down to the subatomic particles — why are they arranged thus, now?

This is just like the cup on the desk, except that the **existence** of the thing, not its location, is at stake: the coffee’s existence depends on the water’s, the water’s on an actualized potential of its atoms, theirs on one of their particles. That is a **hierarchical series of actualizers of existence**, and so it must have a first member.

summary.heading: The unactualized actualizer
summary.body:
The first member must actualize other things’ existence **without its own existence needing actualization**. So it has no potential for existence at all; it is always, already actual — it doesn’t just *have* actuality but **is pure actuality**. It doesn’t merely happen to lack a cause; it couldn’t even in principle need one, since nothing in it could be actualized. It is an **uncaused cause**: Aristotle’s **Unmoved Mover**, or more precisely an **unactualized actualizer**.

The route began not with the universe as a whole but with a cup of coffee. Yet the result applies universally: every material thing — the leaf, the fly, anything with the potential either to exist or not — exists at a moment only if certain potentials are actualized, and so only because an unactualized actualizer is causing it to exist. Retracing the whole route, Feser sums up: from the undeniable fact of change we are led to an Unmoved Mover.

A footnote notes that on Aristotelian **hylemorphism** water isn’t a mere aggregate of atoms (they exist in it only ‘virtually’); its metaphysical constituents are **substantial form** and **prime matter**. The argument can be put in those terms too: matter depends for concrete existence on form and form on matter, so the composite would be an explanatory circle unless something outside it keeps it in being.
